title: Zen Work
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: In Soto Zen Buddhism, work is seen as an essential part of spiritual practice that can bring fulfillment and dignity when approached with mindfulness and effort. By focusing on the process of work itself, rather than its outcome, individuals can cultivate a deeper appreciation for their labor and find greater joy and meaning in their daily activities. This approach involves working with awareness and attention to the present moment, letting go of extra conditions that lead to striving and dissatisfaction, and finding energy and stability in the task at hand.

sentences.text: We thought we'd investigate the Zen style of work tonight, make a few remarks, and then work together.
There are many stories about Zen and work.
Bai Zhang was the Zen master famous for establishing the Zen monastic rules.
When Buddhism came to China, the emphasis changed in multiple ways.
One of them is that the monks were a little less concerned with individual ethical rules and more concerned with collective rules.
Elaborate systems of conduct developed in the monasteries that probably didn't exist in India, and Bai Zhang is credited with establishing a set of monastic rules.
He was apparently very into working.
He would work every day, even though he was the esteemed abbot of the place.
He worked physically in the fields and cleaning the buildings and so on.
He was getting old and seemed to be tired, so the monks felt sorry for him and hid the tools.
He refused to eat.
He went on a hunger strike.
He said, "Why should others work for me?
It was my practice to work."
And he has a famous saying: "A day of no work is a day of no eating."
Another time, a student, Yunyan, asked Bai Zhang, "Every day there's hard work to do.
Who do you do it for?
Why are you working?"
Bai Zhang said, "There is someone who requires it."
Yunyan said, "Why not have him do it himself?"
Bai Zhang said, "He has no tools."
She has no tools.
So somehow we have the tools.
We have the possibility of serving, of working.
Another time, Di Zhang, another Zen teacher, was working in the rice fields.
A monk named Zhuishan came walking up on a pilgrimage.
Di Zhang saw him walking up and asked the obvious question: "Where are you coming from?"
This is one of the great conceits of these stories.
It's probably partly historically true that the monks would train in a monastery all winter and then again all summer.
Then in the spring and the fall, they would go to other monasteries to visit.
How do you get there?
Not on the train.
So they'd walk, sometimes for days or weeks, or maybe a month.
So Di Zhang asked the visiting monk, Zhuishan, "Where do you come from?"
Zhuishan said, "From the south."
Di Zhang said, "How is Buddhism in the south these days?"
Zhuishan said, "There's extensive discussion."
Di Zhang was not impressed.
"How does that compare with me here planting the fields and making rice to eat?"
Zhuishan challenged him.
He said, "Well, what do you do about the world?
You're just here in your farm field.
What are you doing about the rest of the world?"
Di Zhang said, "What do you call the world?"
Really important question for us.
How are we calling the world?
How are we creating the world?
I didn't have a lot of time to prepare the talk, so instead of getting out my koan books, I was Googling away trying to find these koans.
Sometimes that's quicker, sometimes not.
And oddly, one of the top hits was a talk from 1997 by Norman Fischer.
So here are a few paragraphs from Norman Fischer about work.
He was living at Green Gulch at this time.
*But if you really think about what work is, you see that everything is work.
Being alive and in a body is work.
Every day there is eating and shitting and cleaning up.
There's brushing and bathing and flossing.
Every day there's thinking and caring and creating.
So there's no stopping the work and no escaping from the work.
The work is everywhere.
Among students, there's no work time and leisure time.
There's just life time, daytime, nighttime.
Work is deep and dignified.
It's what we were born to do and what we feel the most fulfilled in doing.*
We can forget that, right?
Fulfilling to work.
And he goes on:
*Even within conventional notions of work, there are lots of kinds of work.
Administrative work, clerical work, creative work, emotional work.
All these forms of work are important and useful.
But in religious practice, especially in Zen, there's a special place given to physical work and the dignity of physical work.*
And I think this is really true when the community of practitioners comes together, hand to hand, shoulder to shoulder, to give our bodies together in working.
It's really a good feeling.
I was remembering the astonishing amount of work that we did to get this building ready eight years ago.
We were no bigger or smaller really than we are today.
We looked around, with a group of people deciding to lease the place, and we were like, "Wow, can we really do this?
I don't know."
But somehow many people showed up.
One of the things that was interesting was that some of the people who came most regularly were not the people whom I had been seeing the most often in meditation.
But there are some people in our broader community who could feel somehow, "Here's an expression of practice, to work, to create a temple, a place of practice."
Some of them were incredibly devoted.
Of course, some people were both steady meditators and workers.
We had all different combinations.
So it was really a beautiful thing.
It was a little bit sad in a way, a relief and also a little bit sad when we finished.
We didn't have that work to pull us together.
And people coming later, why would you even think about what had happened before?
In every place and in every community there is a history of work, right?
A history of great effort.
And we can feel it if we're sensitive.
But still, we have plenty of work to do.
We keep the building clean and serviceable.
We've been building the garden in the back.
Little chunks of effort and some interesting lulls.
Training in how to work at the center can really help us significantly in the rest of our life.
The attitude and spirit that we bring to our work is a huge factor in our happiness, in our suffering, in the quality of our existence.
When I was a young man living at the Zen centers at Green Gulch Farm in Tassajara Zen Center, the work was really valuable to me.
I learned lessons there that I'm still trying to develop and learn more thoroughly.
And the main one is so simple.
So simple.
The simple idea that you can start and stop.
That you can actually start and stop.
We train in this by starting and stopping the work at particular times in the schedule.
Jaron here has just been training in this for a year or two.
And this is an incredible thing.
When the bell rings, or the work bell rings, or the drum, sometimes they bang the drum, you go to the work period, you get your assignment, and you work.
When the bell rings to stop work, you put away your tools and you stop.
And you engage fully in the next activity.
So the big difference between that and how we often work is that the focus is on making effort with the task we are engaged in.
Just making effort.
The focus is not on accomplishment or completion.
It helps to train us out of habits we might have, like, "Just a minute, let me just finish this."
That impulse seems honorable on the face of it.
We're doing our work for the benefit of ourselves and others.
The time is up, but we're almost done.
Why not just push a little bit?
Try a little harder.
Get it done.
That would be a good thing.
We want to complete our tasks,
but there's a huge cost to this way of working.
It turns the value of our work into accomplishment of something, and strips the work itself of value.
It puts the energy into results.
Of course, results are basically a figment of our imagination anyway.
We have some projected result, but we don't really know what the real result is of anything.
When the emphasis is on a result, it pulls our energy away from appreciating the doing of our work.
It makes doing unimportant and makes accomplishment important.
Then we soon see how endless that treadmill can be.
The mind is good at adding more conditions to what constitutes an accomplishment or completion.
So we're always scrambling.
There's always a little more we could do.
It's not quite good enough, right?
We should try it again.
Remember that in the seven factors of enlightenment we studied last year, three of them are energy, joy, and samadhi, which means concentration or stability of the mind.
Energy, joy, and stable mind.
Working with an appreciation for the feeling of the moment and the doing of the work, the pleasure in the actual working itself, supports these factors.
This can be energizing and joyful and stable.
Whereas reaching so hard for accomplishment is destabilizing and not too joyful, and saps our energy, makes us exhausted.
Working with an appreciation for the work itself also supports our mindfulness practice in very practical ways.
We practice coming back to what's happening now.
What am I doing now?
What's the feeling of this moment?
Instead of our mind going to some imagined end point.
So work can be a real training in being present.
Our approach to work can also reveal a lot about our mind.
Sometimes we look at work that needs doing and aversion arises.
We don't want to do something that needs to be done.
Sometimes we do it anyway, trying to rush through it and not notice the feeling of it.
Other times we do it resentfully, or we just try to avoid doing it altogether, hoping it will go away.
I felt that here the other day, Saturday, well, not recently, and then I noticed something about it on Saturday.
We made this huge effort and raised a lot of money to build our garden in the back parking lot.
Before we began, I had noticed that there were horsetails, little weeds in the cracks right on the edges of the foundation.
We didn't really think about it beyond that.

Then we carefully dumped 20 yards of soil on top of those horsetails and started watering gently and perfectly with our drip irrigation system, creating ideal conditions for plant life, which is good for all kinds of plants and really good for horsetails, really good for horsetails.
Horsetails are ancient.
They are much older than the flowering plants, and have been here long before mammals.
So we're helping our ancestors back there.
But we really don't want to have a garden of only horsetails They quickly will make it that way.
I was looking at this the other day and I was really bummed out.
I was angry, disappointed in myself, disappointed in the others.
Why didn't we get rid of those?
Why didn't we get more advice from wise gardeners?
We plowed ahead.
None of the main people involved have degrees in landscaping or anything like that.
We're just a bunch of guys with rocks and gals with soil.
Some people gave us money and we wouldn't spend it.
So I felt like, God, we blew it here.
We really blew it, and there's no way out.
We'll be forever pulling horsetails.
And darn it, we don't have many people out there pulling horsetails either, and it's just getting worse and worse.
Then I was working during the work period on Saturday morning during the retreat with Matt.
Matt was expressing his great joy at getting to work in a garden.
I guess he lives in an apartment or something, and he doesn't have a garden.
He spoke of how satisfying and easy it was to pull the horsetails out of the ground, how fun it was to have the sense of accomplishment, and how he cleaned up a little area.
He asked me, "Would you mind if I came here on my own and weeded in the garden?
Would that be okay?
Because I'd really appreciate getting to do that."
And of course I flipped my attitude right around.
I realized that things are as they are.
Horsetails are here.
Taxes are here.
Gardens are here.
Houses need painting.
Old barns are here.
And we have in front of us the opportunity to express our love for the world and our ability to work.
Just like Dijon said, there is someone who requires it of us.
We're the ones with the tools.
We're the ones with the opportunity.
So tonight I thought we'd go a little more into detail around the particulars of organizing Zen work and the spirit of Zen work.
We're going to try to have a work period on Wednesday night, maybe once a month, and that will free up Saturday morning.
Well, we already have a work period.
Did you know that?
Every Saturday morning there's already a short work period.
There's usually just a few of us.
We run around and clean the toilets and sweep and run out of time.
So even in those periods, we're going to focus a little more on how to do this work with a good feeling, but just logistically.
If we use the Wednesday night vast crowd... but we have plenty of people.
Plenty of people.
We'll be able to get more done and train and work so it will benefit our life.
So here are a few pointers.
I'll record this too, and the other people can hopefully listen.
In the work period, the work leader is a very important person.
We haven't fully activated our work leaders yet, mostly for want of thinking about it and talking about it and training in this.
I think I more or less have assumed that someone would read my mind for 30 years.
So now we're ready, or I'm ready, to say it out loud.
It's best if the work leader spends a little bit of time ahead.
It's not a huge obligation.
It's best if the work leader has thought about the tasks that need doing, and has double-checked that the tools and materials are at hand.
One of the things the work leader is really trying to do is honor the power and potential of six or eight or 20 people working for however long it is.
Tonight we'll work for maybe 45 minutes, and there's about two, four, six, eight, 12 of us here.
So that's like nine hours of work.
That's like you came here and put in a nine-hour day.
We can do that together if we don't waste any time.
So that's the work leader's obligation: to honor that potential.
There's a potential here for great activity, so the work leader wants to be organized.
The work meeting should be brief.
It's not a time for dialogue.
It's a time for the work leader to assign tasks in a very clear way.
So the work leader has thought a little bit about what they're going to say, and it should be almost all communication from the work leader to the workers.
If a lot of discussion is needed, then we need to refine just a little bit more for next time.

A quick question, no big deal, but it's not ideal if the workers are going to say, "No, wait a minute, where is that?" or "Actually, no, I don't think I can do that," or "Oh, you know what, I'm sorry, I've got to go."
Would you please clean the toilets?
Off you go.
The work leader also can have some awareness, and the workers can remind the work leader about their own limitations and abilities.
So it's perfectly appropriate if the work leader says, "Would you please clean the toilets?" and you say, "I'm sorry, but I have an injury in my back.
Can I please have another task?"
Or something like this.
It's also best if the work leader does assign the tasks instead of asking for volunteers.
This is a little counterintuitive, because it seems like a nice task for volunteers.
It's friendly: wouldn't someone like to volunteer?
It's very friendly.
Part of the great power and potential of work period, though, is that you might get a task you really don't like, and there's something to be learned from that.
Our work together is not about our own personal preferences.
It's also not about what we're good at, necessarily.
We don't necessarily want to assign the best person to the job, which is also counterintuitive.
We want to work like we're one body.
We're not going to chop off our non-dominant hand just because we've got a bunch of dominant hands around.
So it's great if the work leader has their list of tasks and just goes around the circle and says, "Would you do this?
Would you do this?
Would you please do this?"
As you receive your task, you can begin your work.
If you have a question, you can ask.
It's fine.
So then we have our assignments, ideally within a couple of minutes.
Even 20 or 30 people can have all their assignments in a couple of minutes.
Then we get our tools and begin our work.
When working, our intention is to work steadily and quietly, only talking if it's essential to talk.
And just as well, I didn't correct Matt about this because I got a great teaching from him, but he shouldn't have been talking to me then.
Sorry, Matt.
One of the nice rules of thumb is to only talk if you're speaking about that which you can see in front of you.
That helps you realize, "Oh, I'm talking about something else, some other time or place or abstraction."
We want to work steadily, keeping in motion, but not rushing.
There's a discernment there.
Not too slow.
This is not a slow, careful thing.
We're working, but not rushing.
When our task is finished, we should either find another task or ask the work leader for new work.
The idea is that everyone in our one body is working steadily until the ending time.
This is also a little different from some other ways of organizing work.
We wouldn't say, "Oh, I worked really good and fast and I'm efficient, I'm a good bathroom cleaner, I got everything done.
And look, they made coffee.
I'm going to have a little coffee while they finish up their tasks," and sit there while everyone else is running around.
That would actually make sense in some contexts, but here it does not.
We all just keep working until the end of the work period.
One of the skills of the work period is to become more aware of the undone tasks all around us.
If we finish our bathrooms and we don't see the work leader close by, we start wiping down baseboards or we grab the broom and sweep out back.
We find work to do.
And it's great if, as we become more engaged in work as a community, we start noticing a little more all the time: oh, there's a task undone.
We could do that in the next work period.
We do have many tasks that are done by people coming here individually, and that's a wonderful offering.
That's fantastic.
But I hope more and more we'll be able to do our work together in the work period as training, as Dharma practice.
Other tasks besides cleaning and simple maintenance can happen during work periods.
Maybe there's some sangha responsibility that you have that you're doing off at home.
You could bring that to a work period.
Something clerical, or even a meeting, is work, right?
These are work.
But then it's best to let the work leader know before the meeting.
Would you please assign me and Ken to have a meeting about strategic visioning or something?
That's our most important work.
Sure.
Another thing that's great about work is what an opportunity it is to feel our body in motion, to really hold our attention inside our body, to feel the feeling of operating our tools.
And the last point is the signal to end work: a loud roll down on the clackers, followed by one hit, a pretty slow roll down, like the Han.
It's a little slower than that.

Here at Red Cedar, the work leader should probably do this first downstairs, maybe opening the door if there are people outside so they hear it, and then upstairs, and then we meet back at the lobby in the work circle where we started.
So that's what I wanted to say about work.
Does anyone have any questions?
And think about this point about accomplishment versus activity.
It's pretty subtle.
The mind goes pretty quickly to accomplishment.
We don't always notice that we're actually ignoring the steps we're doing to get there.
Okay, let's close the talk and have a work period.
I'll be the work leader today, but hopefully it'll be someone else next time.
May our intentions equally exc...
